This is crazy: 

The Spanish Supreme Court (Contentious-Administrative Chamber, Section V) confirmed on July 8, 2026 that applying "devoluciones en caliente" (immediate pushbacks) to migrants arriving by sea is illegal, notably for those attempting to reach Sebta or Melilla by swimming.

The ruling was made public on July 8, 2026, then widely circulated on July 10 by the General Council of the Judiciary (CGPJ) and the Spanish legal press.

This ruling certainly encouraged the first migrants to attempt the crossing to Sebta. The maritime route to Sebta, undertaken by swimming, is dangerous because of the presence of very powerful currents. This morning, four deaths and some twenty missing were reported [the source text reads "cingtaine," most likely "vingtaine," about twenty, though possibly "cinquantaine," about fifty].

The provision of Spanish immigration law authorizing immediate pushbacks applies only when a migrant attempts to cross "physical elements of border containment."

In other words, the Sebta fence, the Melilla fence, and physical barriers.

The sea, by contrast, is not an element of containment. The Court specifies that drones, cameras, radars, and sensors do not substitute for a physical barrier. A migrant intercepted at sea therefore cannot be returned immediately without an individual administrative procedure.

The ruling stems from an appeal brought by an Algerian national who was intercepted at sea while attempting to reach Sebta by swimming, then immediately returned to Morocco.

The lower courts had already ruled in his favor. The Supreme Court now confirms this interpretation and unifies Spanish case law.

Since this decision, persons arriving by sea must be identified, must undergo an individual administrative procedure, and can no longer simply be handed back across the border minutes after their arrival.

https://t.co/IIo2ZPnPbH

tweets.text:
Everyone assumes @Ondo owns tokenized stocks.

But today, it's a lot more competitive than you think.

Total value of tokenized stocks grew from $290M to $1.9B during the 2025/26 period, but the bigger change is how much more competitive the market became.

Here's how it fragmented ↓

1. Platforms

In January 2025, @Securitize made up 94.6% of the market.

Today, its share is down to 13%. Current leaders:
• @Ondo: 45.5%
• @xStocksFi: 25.9%

2. Networks

At the start of 2025, nearly all tokenized stock value sat on @Algorand.

Right now:
• Ethereum: 35.9%
• Solana: 18.7%
• BNB Chain: 16.3%

Tokenized stocks are no longer tied to one network.

3. Holders

From 2025 to 2026, wallets holding tokenized stocks grew from 57K to 752K.

Robinhood now accounts for 44% of holders but only 2.3% of total value, while Ondo has fewer holders and much more capital per wallet.

The leaders are different depending on what you measure:

@RobinhoodApp wins distribution.
@Ondo wins capital.
@xStocksFi wins activity.

Tbh, I find this much healthier than one platform and one chain owning almost the entire category.

It signals a maturing market.

Imagine being able to loop Bitcoin the way people loop ETH or stablecoins.

You stake BTC for a base yield, borrow against it, deploy that capital somewhere else, and keep earning underneath the whole time.

Which is kinda strange when you think about it.

$BTC is the biggest pool of capital in crypto and most of it does nothing, mainly because the yield options have meant handing your coins to a custodian or wrapping them.

Stacks has been building towards that kind of setup for a while.

Self-custodial Bitcoin Staking first, then liquid products on top like stBTC so the position can actually move through lending and trading instead of sitting stuck.

Its Q2 report shows the surrounding ecosystem is starting to look ready for it:

• 110K+ new wallets, up roughly 50% from Q1
daily users up around 55%, past 1.6M cumulative wallets
• Zest at $70M TVL, 1,500+ liquidations with no bad debt
• BitFlow past $5B cumulative transaction value
• Hermetica's latest 75 BTC hBTC allocation filled in a day

Stacking DAO also announced stBTC, which is meant to let BTC keep earning staking yield while remaining liquid enough to use elsewhere.

The part I find interesting is what this could eventually lead to.

Not just earning a few percent on idle BTC, but building proper Bitcoin strategies around it: lending, looping, trading, and whatever comes next.

Q3 is where we start finding out how much demand there really is for that.

Glad to partner with @Stacks on this one.

tweets.text:
We spent 2 years calling Chinese AI models "cheap copycats."

Last week something changed the space forever, and almost nobody in crypto is connecting it to DeAI yet.

What happened? Kimi K3.

Moonshot released Kimi K3 for anyone to download and run.

It's the biggest open model ever released, and independent rankings put only three models on the planet ahead of it (all closed American models such as Claude and GPT).

The difference is money. Chinese open models are running 60 to 90% cheaper than Claude and GPT.

And developers have already switched. On OpenRouter (the platform devs use to access AI models), Chinese models now handle 3x more traffic than American ones.

A year ago it was the reverse.

How does this affect DeAI?

Open models are the backbone of DeAI. Training new models in a decentralized way is still too hard, so most DeAI projects today are really doing one thing: running open models and selling access to them.

So the bet looks like this:

Better open models → more demand to run them → a bigger market for DeAI to compete for.

But let's be real: better open models don't mean DeAI automatically wins. Devs can just buy access from big centralized companies instead.

K3 shifts this in DeAI's favor though.

The model is so massive that Moonshot recommends 64+ GPUs just to run it. Nobody's running this at home, which means everyone who wants K3 has to pay someone to run it for them.

That's the market.

And DeAI providers have an angle the centralized guys can't copy: private access with no signups and no KYC. @AskVenice is already offering K3 on exactly that pitch.

There's also a catch in the fine print that most people haven't read.

K3 isn't fully free to use. Any company selling access to K3 needs a separate deal with Moonshot once they make over $20m a year.

And that $20m counts everything the company makes, not just what they make from K3.

We spent 2 years calling Chinese AI models "cheap copycats."

Last week something changed the space forever, and almost nobody in crypto is connecting it to DeAI yet.

What happened? Kimi K3.

Moonshot released Kimi K3 for anyone to download and run.

It's the biggest open model ever released, and independent rankings put only three models on the planet ahead of it (all closed American models such as Claude and GPT).

The difference is money. Chinese open models are running 60 to 90% cheaper than Claude and GPT.

And developers have already switched. On OpenRouter (the platform devs use to access AI models), Chinese models now handle 3x more traffic than American ones.

A year ago it was the reverse.

How does this affect DeAI?

Open models are the backbone of DeAI. Training new models in a decentralized way is still too hard, so most DeAI projects today are really doing one thing: running open models and selling access to them.

So the bet looks like this:

Better open models → more demand to run them → a bigger market for DeAI to compete for.

But let's be real: better open models don't mean DeAI automatically wins. Devs can just buy access from big centralized companies instead.

K3 shifts this in DeAI's favor though.

The model is so massive that Moonshot recommends 64+ GPUs just to run it. Nobody's running this at home, which means everyone who wants K3 has to pay someone to run it for them.

That's the market.

I think $AAPL will guide September revenue inline to slightly higher than the Street.

That outlook will be impacted by two new forces, a headwind of the likely shift to a staggered iPhone release schedule over the next six months, and the tailwind of the price increase.

I expect the net of those should results in the overall revenue guide for September to be inline to slightly better than the Street, which now sits up 12% y/y.

My optimistic outlook may come across as aggressive considering the high bar, with the Street looking for 21% iPhone growth in June, and 18% in September, compared to the segment that was up on average 2% per year from FY22-FY25.

The reason for my optimism:
1. iPhone is riding the upgrade wave from the FY21 monster 39% growth.

2. The staggered upgrade schedule will force people who have historically bought the new lower priced model and need a phone now to trade up to a Pro model. I expect fractional at best shipments of the foldable phone in September.

3. The price increase will likely average 15%. While that jump will soften demand, the next effect should still be a net positive.

Most people are getting poorer and they have no idea why.

Their salary goes up, their bank balance doesn't shrink… On paper they’re fine.

But things like property, stocks, and land run away from you. And every year the gap gets wider.

Here's what’s happening:

Wages grow at the pace of the economy. Assets grow at the pace of liquidity... about 8% a year.

Own assets, the tide carries you up. Don't, and you spend your life running to stand still.

And it's deliberate. Banks, central banks and the treasury are the only ones who can create money, and they create it to fund the interest on their debt. That money floods in and lifts every asset with it.

Debasement, or liquidity if you want the nicer word. That's the force under everything.

I think this is massively underappreciated. LLMs still generalize surprisingly badly. A teenager can learn to drive with maybe 30 hours of practice and then handle roads and situations they have never seen before. An AI system needs an absurd amount of driving data (like trillions of hours!), simulation and edge cases to achieve the same reliability.

And this is true in basically every field. Coding, biology, finance, healthcare, office work. As long as models cannot generalize from a few examples like humans do, we will need gigantic amounts of high quality, task-specific and verifiable data just to teach them what we consider basic work.

Compute gets most of the attention, but data is just as important and it's getting more and more expensive.
